title: Resolve the certify-key source (device-link struct +0x330): password-derived or cloud-issued?
description: The make-or-break question for cloud-free control (from te-qgj.4). The IoTVideo certify handshake encrypts the app's 32-byte R1 with a 16-byte per-device key held in the device-link struct at offset +0x330. If it derives from the device password, TianEye can complete the handshake locally; if the cloud issues it, full P2P impersonation is out. Trace where +0x330 is written (device-add/login/nSetDevicePwd path and the service messages that populate a device link), or capture a real handshake (te-2dc) and test reproducibility from the password. Also trace the check-LAN-password message format (iv_check_set_lan_device_pwd) as a possible password-only LAN auth.
close_reason: RESOLVED: the IoTVideo certify key is derived from the cloud-issued ACCESS TOKEN, not the device password. iv_set_access_token hex-decodes the accessToken into a 64-byte blob at term+0x300 (decoded token starts with 0x02); the 16-byte certify key is at offset 0x30 (+0x330) and is re-keyed on every token set/refresh (iv_update_access_id_token). So completing the IoTVideo P2P handshake requires a valid cloud-issued token - the device password alone is insufficient. Verdict for IoTVideo stands: block the cloud, serve media over RTSP/ONVIF; do not impersonate P2P. Documented in protocol-iotvideo.md (crux RESOLVED), cloud-redirect.md, protocol-go-guide.md. Filed follow-up for the only remaining loophole (LAN-password path).

title: IoTVideo application layer: model commands, user data, built-in commands, A/V frames
description: Wire format of nExecuteModelCmd (read/write/action with path + JSON), user data (PTZ JSON), BuiltInCmd payloads (playback, download, thumbnails), and the audio/video frame headers (codec, timestamps, keyframe flags) so frames can be fed to a decoder or RTP packetizer.
close_reason: Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md 'Application Layer'. Model commands (nExecuteModelCmd read/write/take_action) -> GDM data-object message: gute frame magic 0x7F type 0xAA carrying session id, 32-bit msg id, path string + json value string (both length-prefixed as len-1), 0x2A-byte prefix; response matched by msg id with code+data. User data (PTZ/zoom JSON) via iv_send_user_data on an open media channel (needs live session; else model-cmd path). Built-in commands = BuiltInCmd codes + res_codec.c resource pack/unpack. A/V = push-channel frame, 20-byte header (class 3, subtype 8, is-video + keyframe flag bits, length, checksum=hash^len, channel id, session id) wrapping media; media carries opt_video/opt_videoI/source_id/sqnum/pts; large frames fragmented (RtcFrm_FragBeg). H.264/H.265 + G.711 as per RTSP. Open: exact pts/sqnum offsets, response JSON schemas (capture).

title: IoTVideo crypto and certification handshake
description: CertifyReq/CertifyResp/CertifyAck (R1/R2), what keys are used (device password, device key, anonymous app key, server-issued material), frame encryption cipher and key schedule, iv_check_set_lan_device_pwd. Decide whether a client holding only the device password can complete it.
close_reason: Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md 'Crypto and Certification'. Mechanism decoded: session holds RC5-32 schedules - hardcoded bootstrap key 'www.gwell.cc' (base64 d3d3Lmd3ZWxsLmNj, non-secret), a 16-byte per-device certify key at device-link+0x330, and a session key. CertifyReq (type 0x0C) sends a 32-byte random R1 encrypted with the certify key; on CertifyResp the session cipher is keyed from R1 directly (mode-2 RC5). RC5 is standard (canonical P/Q). Found a separate LAN-password check/modify path (iv_check_set_lan_device_pwd -> giot_eif_send_check/modify_lan_pwd) that may allow password-only LAN auth. CRUX UNRESOLVED: whether the +0x330 certify key is password-derived (TianEye can forge) or cloud-issued (cannot); +0x330 is written via a computed pointer, needs more tracing or a capture. Filed te-qgj.8 to resolve. crypto-and-auth.md and cloud-redirect.md cross-linked.

title: IoTVideo session setup: service discovery, server registration, P2P/LAN/relay connect
description: Document how a session starts: GetServiceList request/response, access-server login, device lookup via the index, hole punching, relay fallback, and the LAN path (broadcast table on UDP 8900, nLanDevConnectable). Decode the UDP 8900 search/broadcast packet. Establish whether a LAN or AP-mode session can start with no server.
close_reason: Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md 'Session Setup'. Four stages mapped from native functions/strings: (1) service discovery GET /iotvideo/service/ListService/GetServiceList?serviceId&token returns Asrv (access server) and p2psrv (relay) lists with v4/v6 addrs; (2) register with Asrv (init-info/online msg + 35/40/50s heartbeats), signalling layer keyed {msg_id,tid,path,code,json}; (3) detect fastest p2psrv + CALLING_REQ to wake device + ListNat NAT exchange; (4) MTP session via add_lan_or_nat (LAN/P2P), add_udp_relay or add_tcp_relay (RELAY), matching ConnectionMode. Open: GetServiceList JSON, control-message byte layouts, and whether LAN session works with no servers (all need capture/te-qgj.4).

title: IoTVideo transport: UDP/KCP framing, packet header, message types
description: Decode the libiotvideomulti packet layer: header layout, message type codes, KCP usage (IKCP constants present), fragmentation, keepalive, IPv4/IPv6. Source files named in the binary: gute_session.c, p2pc_chnnel_v2.c, p2pc_comm.c, p2pc_mtpchnnel.c, iot_video_link_app.c.
close_reason: Done: docs/protocol-iotvideo.md (transport layer). gute frame = 24-byte header (magic 0x7E/0x7F, type, uint16 total length, 8-byte id, body-prefix word, 32-bit XOR checksum, flags word) + payload. Flags decoded: zlib bit, encryption mode (0 none / 1 per-frame-key RC5 / 2 session-key RC5), reliability (ack) bits, response/skip-checksum, extended-header and detect bits. Checksum formula captured. Encryption is standard RC5-32 (canonical P/Q constants confirmed), 8-byte blocks, three key schedules (id / per-frame-derived / session); mode 1 is obfuscation since its key comes from the cleartext header. Fragment/detect XOR obfuscation noted. Transport: UDP v4/v6 direct/NAT/LAN or TCP relay, KCP for reliable streams. Open: live-capture confirmation (te-2dc), RC5 round count (te-qgj.4), KCP tuning.

title: Identify which SDK family the test camera speaks (IoTVideo or legacy Gwell)
description: Decides which spec to do first. Evidence so far: no reply to the Gwell UDP 8899 search, nothing broadcast on 8900. Check the device ID format the user sees in the app, TCP 50000 behaviour, and anything else observable on the LAN without the cloud.
close_reason: Test camera is IoTVideo: the user confirmed its device ID is 10+ digits (> 2^32, the app's IoTDeviceUtils.isIoTDevice threshold). Consistent with no reply to the Gwell UDP 8899 search. Rule documented in docs/direct-control.md; README tested-camera row updated. IoTVideo spec (te-qgj.2-.5) goes first.

title: Protocol spec for a Go reimplementation of the Gwell and IoTVideo camera SDKs
description: User request: document libp2pav/libgwmediaplayer (legacy Gwell) and libiotvideomulti (IoTVideo) well enough that TianEye can talk to Yoosee cameras from Go, ideally directly on the LAN with the cloud blocked. Docs only (planning/RE phase): wire formats, state machines, crypto, message catalogues, in our own words in docs/protocol-iotvideo.md and docs/protocol-gwell.md. No decompiled code in the repo. Static analysis with Ghidra on spike/ghidra plus safe probes of the test camera.

title: Document how the app controls a camera directly (LAN / AP mode, no cloud relay)
description: User request. Trace every path where the Android app talks to the camera without the cloud in the middle: AP-mode settings writes, LAN-mode P2P sessions (ConnectionMode LAN), LAN search/discovery, wired setup, and what still needs the cloud first. Record transports, ports and message formats in docs/ in our own words.
close_reason: Done: docs/direct-control.md. Direct paths: LAN-mode P2P (route chosen in native SDK; Java thing-model layer is route-agnostic), legacy Gwell LAN search on UDP 8899 with full request/reply layout, IoTVideo LAN search/broadcast module on UDP 8900 (+ send ports), AP mode (GW_AP_/GW_IPC_ SSIDs, camera = DHCP gateway, whole-object settings writes, no cloud), wired token hand-off, RTSP/ONVIF. Test camera answered neither search and broadcasts nothing unprompted. Whether a LAN session needs the server moved to epic te-qgj.

title: Inventory the test camera's ONVIF services, especially Events (local motion alarms)
description: Gap from the docs review: alarm-delivery.md and local-storage.md assume alarms need the vendor cloud or TianEye's own motion detection, but nobody checked ONVIF. Call GetServices/GetCapabilities on the test camera (port 5000) and record which services answer (Events/PullPoint, Imaging, PTZ, Recording). If Events exists, subscribe and trigger motion to see whether alarms arrive locally. Also try ONVIF PTZ ContinuousMove/Stop if the model has a motor (camera-control.md says untested). Probe only, results go in docs with placeholder IPs.
close_reason: Done: docs/onvif.md. Test camera ONVIF is a thin NVR shim: profiles, stream URIs, device info, network interfaces and encoder config answer (no auth needed); Events (PullPoint and push Subscribe), Imaging, PTZ queries, Stop, snapshot URI and time/NTP are advertised but the server drops the connection. ContinuousMove is acknowledged but the view did not change (PSNR same as noise), so ONVIF PTZ does not work on this unit. Capability XAddrs are shifted by one service and DeviceIO points at a stale address. Alarm-delivery, local-storage, camera-control and README updated: no local alarms via ONVIF on fw 32.01.37.

title: Document how the Android app adds a camera to an account
description: Documentation only, from the decompiled app. Trace the full add-camera flow end to end: the provisioning modes the app offers (QR code shown to the camera, AP hotspot, Bluetooth, smartlink, wired), what each one sends to the camera and how (Wi-Fi credentials, bind token, user/account identifiers, server region), how the bind token is obtained (/openapi/netcfg/cloud/netcfg/genbindtoken), how the app learns the camera came online, the bind call (/openapi/app/user/device/bind fields), and what happens for a camera already bound to another account (forceBind). Note what the camera must do on its side that the app cannot show. Known pieces are scattered in docs/protocol.md and docs/data-inventory.md; this task gives the flow its own doc.
acceptance_criteria: docs/add-camera.md describes each provisioning mode step by step with the data exchanged, the bind-token and bind calls, and open questions, with no device IDs or credentials.
close_reason: Wrote docs/add-camera.md (static, doc-only). Flow: genbindtoken -> hand config to camera -> camera checks in -> poll netcfg devresult every 5 s up to 60x ({devId,status,token}) -> device/bind -> post-setup writes (time zone, openAlert turns cloud video + snapshot upload on, push schedule). Config encodings: QR text <tag><2-hex len><value> (IoTVideo tags 0-5 + APN 6-9; Gwell tags 0-4, no token, owner by numeric account ID) and binary TLV in the AP-mode class (tag 7 time zone, 32 share token). Modes: QR (Wi-Fi password plain text) plus simultaneous MediaTek Elian smart-connection broadcast of SSID+password; AP hotspot via sendMsgToDevice BUILT_IN AP_NET_CONFIG; BLE AES-encrypted via bleAesEncrypt (GATT details in a separate SDK); wired via native LAN search + subscribeDevice; 4G adds APN. Cloud is in the loop for every add. Data inventory updated with the local Wi-Fi exposure.

title: Trace how the app controls PTZ on the camera and document it
description: Known so far (docs/camera-control.md): the live-view screen sends every PTZ move through GwMonitorPlayer.nativePtzControl(direction 0-3) in libgwmediaplayer.so, with an hxstPtzControl(direction, bytes) variant for player mode 4; Action.ptzCheck is PTZ reset/calibration, not movement; the camera's RTSP server advertises a non-standard USER_CMD_SET method and the direction constants are named USR_CMD_OPTION_PTZ_TURN_*. Still to trace: what nativePtzControl sends and over which channel (P2P user data, RTSP USER_CMD_SET, or the TCP 50000 service), the byte layout, whether moves are steps or start/stop, speed, how presets are saved and recalled (PtzControlVM addPreset/selectPreset/deletePreset), zoom/focus (Action.zoomFocusA, ProWritable.zoomFocusW), and the HXST variant. Also check whether the camera's ONVIF ptz_service works for movement, since that would give TianEye a standard path. Verify on the test camera where possible.,
acceptance_criteria: docs/camera-control.md PTZ section describes the command path and message format for move, stop, presets and zoom, states which were verified on the test camera, and says whether ONVIF PTZ works.
notes: Doc-only scope: trace statically; no PTZ commands sent to the camera.
close_reason: Documented in docs/camera-control.md (static, doc-only scope; nothing sent to the camera). Gwell cameras: GwVideoPlayer::ptzControl -> fgSendUserData -> avctl_SendUserData sends a 28-byte P2P user-data frame FF FF FF 88 00 02 <cmd 0x00|0x0C HXST> <dir 0-3> <20-byte payload>, retried 20x/10ms, step only (no stop). IoTVideo cameras: JSON {type:2|22, data:{dir, touchType}} sent as IoTVideo user data with the lens index as the command byte; type 2 = step repeated every 200 ms while held, type 22 = start/stop (touchType 0 press / 1 release), chosen by devSupportPtzNewAgreement. Directions are swapped for mirrored/flipped images. Presets: JSON type 6 {msgId, data:{cmd 0 delete|1 save|2 go-to, idx[], camId}} via live user data or sendMsgToDevice; names/thumbnails live in the cloud. Zoom/focus: Action.zoomFocusA.stVal {actionType zoom|focus _add|_reduce _dn|_up, currentZoom}. ptzCheck = calibration. ONVIF ptz_service exists on the test camera but is unused by the app and untested.

title: Review: validate all RE docs against live captures
description: After the captures exist, check every static claim across docs/ against real traffic: hosts and ports contacted, signing headers on a real request, the P2P service-list exchange, the OTA commands, upload switches and what was actually uploaded. Mark each claim confirmed or refuted on the wire, and fix the docs. Redact device IDs, tokens and IPs from any excerpt.
acceptance_criteria: Each doc in docs/ has its claims marked confirmed/refuted against captures, with no unredacted identifiers.

title: Verdict: can all Chinese-server traffic be redirected or blocked, and how
description: Pull D1 to D6 together into the decision te-cz1 builds on: for every host and hardcoded IP, whether to redirect to TianEye, block, or allow (if anything), the exact DNS entries and firewall rules, what works afterwards, and residual risks (hardcoded IPs, future firmware updates changing hosts, the official app if still used).
acceptance_criteria: docs/cloud-redirect.md has a final rules table (DNS and firewall) and a clear yes/no on whether no data reaches Chinese servers, with the conditions.
close_reason: Appended the final verdict to docs/cloud-redirect.md. Verdict: yes, all China-bound traffic can be stopped - by BLOCKING, not impersonating. Recommended config: (1) firewall block all WAN egress for the camera (hard guarantee, catches hardcoded IPs and DoH); (2) local DNS answering vendor hostnames with TianEye so lookups fail fast / can be emulated; (3) allow only LAN RTSP/ONVIF plus a local NTP. Per-destination rule table (block all cloudlinks.cn/cloud-links.net, block public DNS/NTP, block hardcoded IPs by IP, block OTA). Blocking beats impersonating because it needs no knowledge of camera trust, is verifiable from firewall logs, and TianEye loses nothing (rebuilds video/recording/snapshots from LAN). Residual risk = unconfirmed camera behaviour with cloud blocked, the one must-test-on-hardware item (deferred te-2dc/te-99x.12).

title: Local storage feasibility: can TianEye keep each cloud-stored data type itself
description: Using the data inventory and the upload, event and impersonation findings: for each data type the cloud stores (alarm snapshots, cloud video, event history and AI labels, face database, device settings model, account and device bindings, push), decide whether TianEye can receive and store it locally, what it must emulate (endpoints, keys, certificates), what is impossible without firmware changes, and what is simply lost or not needed. Also list what TianEye can rebuild from the camera itself (RTSP recording, SD playback) instead of copying the cloud.
acceptance_criteria: docs/local-storage.md ends with a per-data-type table: keep locally (how) / rebuild from camera / not possible (why) / not needed.
close_reason: Wrote docs/local-storage.md (synthesis, doc-only). Per-data-type verdict: live video + continuous recordings = rebuild from camera via RTSP/ONVIF (PROVEN, already working); alarm snapshots = grab frame from stream on alarm (feasible) or receive camera upload (unknown, te-99x.10); cloud HLS recordings = not needed (own recording replaces); settings model = keep locally if control channel reachable; bindings = TianEye's own data; face/bird AI = can't copy vendor's server-side model, could run own detector (separate work); PTZ presets = positions on camera, names/thumbnails local; push = replace with own notifications. Bottom line: everything that matters is rebuildable from the camera's LAN interfaces, not copied from cloud; only vendor server-side AI and anything needing to win the P2P session are out, and neither blocks the core goal (RTSP/ONVIF suffice).

title: Trace alarm event delivery and whether TianEye can receive events directly
description: Alarm notifications go camera to cloud to push service (FCM, HMS, offlinePush) to the app. Trace the camera-to-cloud event message (protocol, fields: alarm type, time, image reference, AI labels), the push-token registration endpoints, and whether events also reach the app directly over LAN P2P. Decide whether TianEye can receive events itself so no push goes through Chinese servers.
acceptance_criteria: docs/local-storage.md has an alarm-delivery section: the camera event message format, and whether a local server can receive it (with evidence).
close_reason: Wrote docs/alarm-delivery.md (static, doc-only). Every alarm is cloud-relayed, not camera-to-phone over LAN. App connected: IoTVideo SDK callbacks onReceiveEvent/onReceiveOnlineMsg/onReceivePassthroughMsg via MessageMgrInternal; screens register through IBackstageTaskApi.addPassthroughMsgListener. App closed: push notification parsed to IoTPush {push_type DevAlmTrg|MsgCenter, content, push_data{DevId,EvtId,TrgTime,TrgType}}; richer PushAlarm adds alarmId, alarmType, bucketName (snapshot bucket), deviceId. Token registration: pushTokenBind, offlinePush/uploadToken, push/setting/getAll + setDevOfflineNotifyEna, plus SDK nRegisterOfflinePush. Push services: FCM primary + Huawei HMS and other vendor SDKs by handset. Legacy Gwell: vRetAlarm/vRetAlarmWithTime/vRetAlarmCodeStatus/vRetBindAlarmId JNI callbacks while connected. For TianEye: receiving alarms cloud-free requires standing in as the camera's server (te-99x.10); camera-side alarm report format needs a capture (deferred te-2dc).

title: Trace how the camera uploads alarm snapshots and cloud video
description: From captures (te-ab8) and the app's cloud-playback code: where the camera sends alarm snapshots and video, how it learns the destination (fixed host, URL or credentials handed out by the cloud API, Tencent COS presigned URLs), how it authenticates, and how video is packaged and encrypted (HLS TS segments, AES key from /vas/cloudstorage/getTsEncryptKey). If the destination comes from a cloud API answer, a local server could hand out a local destination instead.
acceptance_criteria: docs/local-storage.md describes the snapshot and video upload flows end to end, marking which steps a local server would need to answer.
notes: Doc-only scope: inferred from what the app fetches back; camera-side upload not visible in the app.
close_reason: Wrote docs/camera-uploads.md (static, doc-only; camera-side upload leg not visible in the app). Snapshots: app builds image URL as server-supplied imgUrlPrefix + per-event suffix (+ thumbUrlSuffix), no decryption, no storage domain hardcoded anywhere; PushAlarm.bucketName points to an object-storage bucket. Cloud video: HLS with AES-128 segments; /vas/playback/play(v2) returns {url m3u8, startTime, endflag}; IoTHLSUtils parses EXT-X-KEY (keyUri, IV); key from /vas/cloudstorage/getTsEncryptKey. Full VAS media API table (events, recordings, speed playback, album, faces) over the HTTP-over-P2P proxy. Open: camera upload host/auth/format and who encrypts segments.

title: Determine whether a local server can impersonate each cloud service to the camera
description: Redirecting a connection only helps if the camera accepts our server. For each cloud connection the camera makes (from captures), work out the protocol (HTTPS, plain HTTP, Gwell UDP/KCP P2P, MQTT, etc.) and what authenticates the server: TLS certificate validation, pinned keys, RSA keys in the P2P handshake, signed responses, or nothing. Test HTTPS endpoints with a self-signed certificate. This decides whether full emulation (te-cz1) is possible or whether only blocking is.
acceptance_criteria: docs/cloud-redirect.md has a per-connection table: protocol, server authentication, and verdict (can impersonate / cannot / unknown, with evidence).
notes: Doc-only scope: answer from static analysis (TLS handling, P2P handshake keys); no self-signed certificate test.
close_reason: Wrote docs/cloud-redirect.md (static, app-side; camera trust decisions are in firmware, deferred). Per-connection verdicts: HTTP-tier services (registration, config, service discovery, P2P index, OTA metadata) likely impersonable pending the camera's TLS trust store, since no pinning exists app-side and request signing (HMAC-SHA1) proves client not server; answering service discovery also steers the P2P layer. P2P media/control session is the crux - opens with R1/R2 mutual certification (CertifyReq/Resp/Ack, RC5, RSA); impersonable only if keyed by device password/ID (which the owner has) vs a baked-in vendor key (unknown). Push is replaced not impersonated. Firmware download serveable but flashing depends on an image signature check. Key point: TianEye doesn't need to win P2P - it serves media over RTSP/ONVIF directly and only needs cloud P2P impersonated OR blocked. Open questions all require firmware (te-99x.12) or capture (te-2dc).

title: Test: redirect all cloud hostnames to a local server with DNS
description: Run local DNS (dnsmasq, Pi-hole or similar) that answers every host from the outbound inventory with the TianEye host's IP, while blocking all other WAN egress for the camera. Find out whether the camera honours DHCP-provided DNS, uses hardcoded resolvers or DoH, or falls back to hardcoded IPs when names do not work. Log what connects to the TianEye host (ports, protocols, first bytes).
acceptance_criteria: docs/cloud-redirect.md states, per host, whether DNS redirection catches it, and lists any traffic that bypasses DNS and needs a firewall rule instead.

title: Test: what still works with all of the camera's internet access blocked
description: Simplest way to send nothing to Chinese servers: block all WAN egress for the camera at the router and allow LAN only. Record what still works and what breaks: RTSP, ONVIF, LAN P2P from the app, SD recording, motion alarms, time (NTP) sync, and reboot behaviour (does it hang or retry hard when it cannot reach the cloud). Log every blocked connection attempt (destination IP/port) from the firewall as a by-product.
acceptance_criteria: A section in docs/cloud-redirect.md listing each feature as works/broken with egress blocked, plus the blocked-destination log summary (redacted).

title: Data inventory: document every data item the app and camera send to the cloud
description: Consolidate into docs/data-inventory.md what leaves the network, per item: what it is, sender (app or camera), host, trigger, and sensitivity. Known so far: login identifiers and password, uniqueId and device info on every request, bind data (device ID, serial, time zone, optional GPS latitude/longitude, camera LAN IP), push tokens, Sensors Data analytics (datasink), Bugly crash logs, ad and Firebase SDK telemetry, PTZ preset snapshots, feedback logs and pictures, alarm snapshots, cloud video, cloud-AI images and the face database, OTA version checks, P2P registration (device ID, LAN/WAN addresses). Also check whether Wi-Fi SSID/password from provisioning ever reaches the cloud. Static now; te-ab8 and te-2dc refine it.
acceptance_criteria: docs/data-inventory.md lists each data item with sender, host, trigger and sensitivity, and marks which are confirmed on the wire versus static only.
close_reason: Wrote docs/data-inventory.md: every data item leaving the LAN, app-side and camera-side, with host, trigger, sensitivity and source. Highlights: login password+uniqueId; bind sends GPS latitude/longitude and the camera's LAN IP; PTZ preset snapshots and feedback pics/logs uploaded; analytics/telemetry/crash/ad SDKs. Confirmed app does NOT send live video, recordings, screenshots, or Wi-Fi credentials (provisioning is local AP/BLE/QR/smartlink). Camera-side: alarm snapshots, cloud video, cloud-AI face DB, alarm events, firmware, legacy SMTP email. 'Confirmed on wire' column left for te-ab8/te-2dc.

title: Document every domain and IP address used, and how each is used
description: Sweep the Java sources and all native libraries (not only the six in Ghidra) for hostnames, URLs and hardcoded IPv4/IPv6 literals, including P2P fallback server IPs, DNS servers (e.g. hardcoded 8.8.8.8 or 114.114.114.114), NTP servers and DoH endpoints. For each one, document how it is used: which feature or code path, whether the app or the camera contacts it, protocol and port, when it is contacted (startup, login, live view, alarm, periodic, debug builds only), and what data goes to it. Classify each by operator and country: Gwell cloudlinks.cn and cloud-links.net, Tencent (qq.com, IoTVideo), ad/analytics SDKs, other. A .cn TLD is not the only marker of a Chinese server. DNS cannot redirect hardcoded IPs, so list them separately. Camera-side hosts come later from firmware (te-99x.12) and captures (te-2dc); add them to the same tables with their source.
acceptance_criteria: docs/cloud-endpoints.md has a complete domain table and a separate IP table. Every row gives operator, country, app or camera, protocol/port, feature and trigger, data sent, and source (static app, firmware, or capture).
close_reason: Rewrote docs/cloud-endpoints.md from the app's authoritative ReleaseHostUrl config (ci/a.java). Full production domain table (20+ hosts: openapi-iot, list.iotvideo, p2p1-10, vasapi, saas-playback, upg1, res.zhiduodev, collect, datasink, advertise, trade, customer-service, agent, personalinfo, faq/help, api1-4, list, abroad, gwell.cc) each with port, how-used, when, operator. Separate hardcoded-IP table (114DNS ping check, Unicom login SDK 123.125.99.31, debug ad/notice IPs) noting none are DNS-redirectable. Test/debug hosts and third-party telemetry/ad domains listed separately. OIDs and version strings excluded as noise.

title: Measure camera and app uploads on the wire with no cloud subscription
description: Static analysis only says what can be uploaded. With a test camera and phone behind a capture point, log destination hosts and byte counts (upstream vs downstream) while: idle, a motion event fires, live view through the app, and SD playback. Look for sustained upstream traffic or image-sized uploads that the static findings do not explain. Keep pcaps in re/. Only hostnames, sizes and redacted patterns go in docs/privacy-uploads.md.
acceptance_criteria: docs/privacy-uploads.md has a measured section: per scenario, hosts contacted and upstream bytes, and whether any image or video upload was observed without a subscription.

title: Trace what the app uploads to remote servers (images, video, logs)
description: Find every path where the Yoosee app sends media or files off the phone: FileResService (resfile/getuploadpath, reportresinfo), cloud storage under /vas/cloudstorage, AI face endpoints (vas/aiface), alarm snapshots, feedback/log upload, and any third-party SDKs (analytics, crash reporting) that send screenshots or files. For each: what is sent, to which host/path, when, and whether it needs a user action or a paid plan. Document in docs/privacy-uploads.md.
acceptance_criteria: docs/privacy-uploads.md has an app-side table: data type, endpoint/host, trigger, opt-in or automatic.
close_reason: App-side uploads documented in docs/privacy-uploads.md. Media leaving the phone: PTZ preset snapshots (Tencent COS or PaaS resfile, when saving a preset) and user-submitted feedback pictures/logs. No app path uploads live video, recordings or screenshots. Log upload and visit log exist but their triggers are not traced (open questions). Server-side face DB, bird images and alarm records point to camera-side uploads, handed to te-e0t.

title: Trace what the camera uploads to the cloud (alarm images, clips, cloud recording)
description: From the device model and server API, work out which camera features push media to Gwell servers: cloud recording (ProWritable._cloudStoage, /vas/cloudstorage), alarm event snapshots and clips (_almEvtSetting, push/alarm endpoints), AI detection and face features, and resfile upload paths handed to the device. notes: Spike code reverted with the rest of the implementation (2026-10-05). The decision and measurements are kept in docs/live-view.md, which was the deliverable.
close_reason: Decision: in-process WebRTC with gortsplib v5 (RTSP pull) + pion v4, video re-packetized but not transcoded; WHEP-style signalling. Proven end to end on the test camera: headless Chrome decoded 1920x1080 @ 15 fps, 0 loss, first frame 1-2 s (keyframe wait), server 1-2% CPU / 24 MB. Key findings: camera RTSP is UDP-only (rejects RTP over TCP); real stream is H.264 Main 15 fps + G.711 A-law 16 kHz (ONVIF claims 30 fps / 8 kHz); camera packs SPS+PPS+IDR into one FU-A NAL with embedded Annex-B start codes, so raw RTP forwarding decodes 0 frames - fixed by decoding to access units and letting pion's payloader re-split. title: Legacy Gwell P2P (libp2pav): session, password encoding, RC5 framing, AV control
description: MTP session setup (LAN/NAT/relay), P2PV1/V2 frame format, P2PGetTreatedPassword and MD5-with-source password encoding, RC5 frame cipher and key, avctl command set (user data incl. the 28-byte PTZ frame), A/V frame format. LAN search on UDP 8899 is already documented in docs/direct-control.md.
close_reason: Done: docs/protocol-gwell.md. Legacy stack shares the gute frame family (RC5-32, XOR checksum), MTP/KCP transport (lan_or_nat/tcp_lan/udp_relay), service discovery /gwellcloud/service/ListService/GetServiceList, UDP 8899 LAN search, avctl_* AV control, 28-byte PTZ frame - all cross-referenced. KEY FINDING: legacy auth password is computable from the device password with no vendor secret - P2PEncryptGW1 = fold(MD5(pw)) into a uint32 (four 32-bit words mod 999999999 XOR a constant table), gated by IsNeedEncrypt (all-digit pws); fgP2PGetMD5PasswordWithSrc = hex MD5; gw_EncodePassword = keyless 17-round LCG. So TianEye can likely authenticate to legacy Gwell cameras with just the device password (unlike the IoTVideo crux). Certify uses RSA session-key exchange but the password check is the auth gate. Open: fold constants/XOR table values, non-numeric path, whether RSA needs a pre-shared camera key (confirm on legacy hardware).

title: Document how the RTSP password relates to the device password
description: Gap from the docs review: README says RTSP uses the device password set in the Yoosee app, but crypto-and-auth.md shows the Connect NVR screen sets a separate RTSP credential (Digest HA1 sent over P2P). Document whether they are the same by default, when they diverge, and what a user must know to give TianEye RTSP access. Static analysis of the app only.
close_reason: Done: crypto-and-auth.md + README. The RTSP credential is NOT the cloud device password. The user sets it on the app's Connect NVR screen (ConnectNVRViewModel.setRTSPPwd), which also toggles rtspEnable/onvifEn. The app sends MD5('admin:HIipCamera:'+pwd) to the camera over the P2P control channel via setRTSPpwd. An RTSP/ONVIF client authenticates with this RTSP password (user admin), not the account password. Newer firmware adds a setRTSPInfo/setNewRTSPPwd account+password variant (creds encrypted in transit) allowing a non-admin username. README camera-table 'Password' row corrected.

title: Find the legacy Gwell firmware update server in libgwmediaplayer.so
description: Legacy cameras update through the JNI calls nCheckDeviceUpdate and nDoDeviceUpdate in libgwmediaplayer.so, which was not in the Ghidra import. Import it, follow those two exports, and record the update-check URL or host, the request format, and how the firmware download URL is built or returned.
acceptance_criteria: docs/ota-firmware.md legacy section names the update host/path and how the firmware URL is obtained, or states what static analysis could not resolve.
close_reason: libgwmediaplayer.so holds no update server for legacy cameras: nCheckDeviceUpdate/nDoDeviceUpdate/nCancelDeviceUpdate take no arguments and only build P2P commands for the camera (fgCheckDeviceUpdate etc.). Replies give current and available versions packed as a.b.c.d ints. The camera picks its update server, so the host comes from the capture task te-cyj. Also found and documented legacy alarm-email (SMTP) settings in docs/privacy-uploads.md.

title: Get firmware download URLs from the IoTVideo upgrade query (sdk/dev/upg/app/queryVersion)
description: The app's deprecated version lookup returns a downUrl field per device (see docs/ota-firmware.md). The app never reads it, but the server still sends it. Trace HttpViaP2PProxy and nHttpProxyRequest in libiotvideomulti.so to find which server and path the proxied request really reaches, and whether it can be called as plain HTTPS with the signing in docs/protocol.md. Then document how to request downUrl for a given tid and currentVersion. Only a placeholder tid goes in docs.
acceptance_criteria: docs/ota-firmware.md names the real endpoint (host, path, auth) behind sdk/dev/upg/app/queryVersion and how to get downUrl from it, or explains why it cannot be called outside the P2P SDK.
close_reason: Static answer documented in docs/ota-firmware.md: sdk/dev/upg/app/queryVersion is not HTTPS from the phone. The app passes (method, url, data) to nHttpProxyRequest; libiotvideomulti wraps it as HTTP_PROXY/REQ with body {http:{url,type},data} and sends it over the SDK's encrypted server link, so it cannot be replayed with curl. Follow-up task filed to capture downUrl from the app with Frida/logs.

title: Trace OTA firmware version check and update flow
description: Determine how the app detects new firmware for a camera and triggers an update. Find: the API endpoint or P2P command used to query available versions (Action._otaVersion is known), the response format (version string, URL, changelog), how the firmware file URL is constructed, and what triggers the check (manual, periodic, or on device connect).
notes: Correction (later the same day): the 20-minute timer is an upgrade watchdog that starts after _otaUpgrade is acknowledged, not a periodic version poll. Also, _otaVersion returns the newest version the camera can install, and the camera fetches firmware itself; the app-side downUrl is never read. See the rewritten docs/ota-firmware.md.
close_reason: Traced full IoTVideo OTA version check flow: Action._otaVersion TAKE_ACTION returns ActionStrValue{version}, polled every 20min via timerGetDeviceVersion. Update availability checked via sdk/dev/upg/app/queryVersion over P2P HTTP proxy. Documented in docs/ota-firmware.md.

title: Trace OTA firmware download and installation
description: Determine how firmware is downloaded to the camera. Find: the download URL format and host domain, whether the binary is pulled from a CDN/cloud URL or pushed via the P2P channel, the installation command (Action._otaUpgrade is known), any checksum or signature verification before apply, and what the camera does on success/failure (reboot signal, rollback).
close_reason: Traced firmware download flow: version check returns downUrl (CDN URL) in VersionInfo.Version bean. Camera downloads firmware autonomously after app sends Action._otaUpgrade TAKE_ACTION. Progress reported as ActionIntValue{0-100, negative=error}. Legacy path uses nCheckDeviceUpdate/nDoDeviceUpdate JNI via libgwmediaplayer.so. Documented in docs/ota-firmware.md.

title: Trace PTZ control commands to camera
description: Determine how pan/tilt/zoom commands are sent to the camera. Identify the command format (HTTP API, proprietary P2P message, ONVIF), the channel used (cloud relay vs. direct LAN), command encoding, and any ACK/response expected. Source likely in the PTZ/joystick UI code and P2P SDK message definitions.
close_reason: Legacy path: nativePtzControl(0=LEFT,1=RIGHT,2=UP,3=DOWN) via avctl_SendUserData in libp2pav. IoTVideo path: TAKE_ACTION on path=Action.ptzCheck. Documented in docs/camera-control.md.

title: Trace remote playback and recording retrieval
description: Determine how the app requests recorded footage from the camera SD card or cloud storage. Identify: the API or P2P message used to list recordings by date/time, the protocol for streaming stored footage (seek, fast-forward), and whether recordings are pulled direct from camera or via cloud relay.
close_reason: Full SD playback command set found: GET_DATE_LIST, GET_LIST_V2V3, STREAM_BEGIN, SEEK, PAUSE, RESUME, SPEED, DOWNLOAD_REQUEST/_DATA. Cloud uses HLS with AES keys from /vas/cloudstorage/getTsEncryptKey. Documented in docs/camera-control.md.

title: Trace camera settings API (resolution, motion, alerts)
description: Determine how the app reads and writes camera configuration: video resolution, motion detection zones and sensitivity, alert schedules, night-vision mode, and audio. Identify whether settings go through the cloud API (/openapi/ paths) or direct P2P messages to the device, and document the field names and value enumerations.
close_reason: All writable property paths found in ProWritable: videoParam, guardParm, motionZone, rtspEnable, recordParam, almEvtSetting, etc. Action paths: ptzCheck, formatTF, cameraOn, zoomFocusA. Documented in docs/camera-control.md.

title: Consolidate findings into a protocol spec for the local server
description: Pull docs/cloud-endpoints.md and the docs/protocol.md sections into one coherent spec: the hostnames to redirect, the minimum set of endpoints/messages TianEye must implement, auth/crypto constraints, and open questions needing live capture to confirm. This is the handoff to the local Gwell-compatible server work.

title: LAN discovery of Yoosee cameras (ONVIF WS-Discovery)
description: Find cameras on the LAN via ONVIF WS-Discovery, then fall back to probing port 554/5000 on a user-given subnet. Capture any Yoosee-specific broadcast seen during the inventory.
notes: Code reverted at the user's request on 2026-10-05: the project is in the planning and reverse-engineering phase, so no implementation is kept yet. Closed as out of scope for this phase; reopen when implementation starts. Findings that survive are in docs/ and README.
close_reason: internal/discovery: Scanner.Scan probes RTSP 554 + ONVIF 5000 across a CIDR, fingerprints Yoosee by the RTSP 401 Digest realm HIipCamera and reads model/firmware from unauthenticated ONVIF GetDeviceInformation; Probe implements ONVIF WS-Discovery for models that answer it. Tests with fake RTSP/ONVIF servers pass. Added tianeye -scan CIDR. Live: the test camera (fw 32.01.37) does NOT answer WS-Discovery in any variant (multicast, unicast, port-3702 listener; verified UDP replies reach this host via SSDP), so the port-probe fallback is the working method; a /24 scan took 12s and correctly identified 3 Yoosee cameras and excluded 2 non-Yoosee RTSP/ONVIF devices. Not done: sniffing Yoosee-specific LAN broadcasts (needs packet capture privileges).

title: Research: cloud-free provisioning of factory-reset cameras
description: Deferred until streams work. Reverse-engineer the Gwell setup flow (AP mode, sound-wave pairing, P2P ports) so a reset camera can join Wi-Fi and get a password without the Yoosee app.
notes: Planning/RE phase: static research and documentation only.
close_reason: Documented cloud-free provisioning in docs/add-camera.md (static, planning/RE phase). Finding: getting a reset camera onto Wi-Fi is entirely local in every mode - the QR setup screen drives three channels at once for the same SSID+password (on-screen QR read by the lens; MediaTek Elian smartlink broadcasting it in Wi-Fi packet patterns via libelianjni; sound-wave via EMTMFSDK.sendWifiSet through the phone speaker, liblarksmarkemtmfJNI), plus AP-hotspot and encrypted BLE. A Realtek SimpleConfig lib is bundled but unused. All reproducible without the vendor. But binding still goes through the cloud (genbindtoken/devresult/device/bind), so app-free + cloud-free first-time setup needs the impersonation work (see cloud-redirect.md); Gwell cameras carry no token in the QR (only account ID in tag 3) and may bind with less cloud involvement (unconfirmed). Simplest path: provision once normally, then move behind the egress block.
